newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia state TV shows ill Tudjman playing tennis.
newsitem.headline: Croatia state TV shows ill Tudjman playing tennis.

text.p: Croatian television has shown President Franjo Tudjman playing tennis, watched by members of his cabinet, a move possibly meant to show he is physically fit despite U.S. reports that he has terminal cancer.
The authoritarian leader, 74, long an avid tennis player, returned to the courts on Tuesday night to inaugurate a new Croatian indoor tennis academy in Zagreb.
State television, controlled by Tudjman's nationalist HDZ party, aired footage of a doubles match won by the president, wearing a track suit, and his partner, a former national tennis champ.

Ministers of his government seated along the sidelines watched gravely in what some Croats called a surreal scene reminding them of the former East European Communist era and the leadership cults surrounding aged leaders.

Tudjman seemed reasonably healthy and appeared to have regained weight. He looked weak and gaunt when he went to the United States last month for what U.S. officials said was treatment for stomach cancer.
The Croatian government has been secretive about Tudjman's condition. It has said he had only a stomach ulcer and swollen lymph nodes.
But U.S. officials say they were told that Tudjman, who was treated at a government hospital in Washington, D.C., had only a few months to live.

Tudjman won approval in the West and initial links to the European Union for Croatia by co-sponsoring peace accords among Croats, Moslems and Serbs in old Yugoslavia and building a Western-style democracy at least on paper.
But the autocratic former communist general has long been accused of abusing human and minority rights and of striving to suppress real political opposition and media freedom.

Some analysts say Tudjman's nationalism and repressive impulses have intensified during his illness, with one U.S. official saying he was acting like a "man with nothing to lose who is determined to do what he wants to".
The United States on Tuesday blasted Tudjman for awarding a medal to a former Bosnian Croat army commander indicted for war crimes.

Last weekend Tudjman, in rhetoric reminiscent of Communist regimes, criticised what he claimed was a cabal of Western powers and "internal enemies" -- opposition parties, human rights groups and independent media -- plotting to dethrone him and his party.

The HDZ has been grappling with a steep decline in its popularity -- based on Croatia's 1991 move to independence from Serbian-led Yugoslavia -- and is under pressure to account for alleged corruption and abuses of power.
